section.title: Bryan Cantrill: Sun, Stack Ranking, Competing with AWS, Oxide, and Regrets
section.deck: Bryan Cantrill, a former Sun distinguished engineer and co-founder of Oxide, argues that meaning, team and honest dealing with customers matter more than rank, titles or money.

blocks.text: Bryan Cantrill was a distinguished engineer at Sun Microsystems, later CTO at Joyent, and in 2019 co-founded Oxide. In this interview he argues that titles, ranks and financial independence are weak sources of meaning. In his account, the best periods of his career came from small teams doing work that looked too hard, and from companies that told their customers the truth. He supports this with his experience of Sun's rating and promotion rules, his objection to stack ranking, the Oracle takeover, competing with Amazon, and the founding of Oxide. The closing section reads back some of his old posts and asks about his regrets. All of it is Cantrill's own recollection and opinion. The host's questions set the order.
blocks.heading: Cantrill's view: meaning, team and trust last longer than rank, titles and money

blocks.question: What was the industry like when you started, and was there a FAANG equivalent?
answer: Cantrill says every era has a hot group of companies. In the 1960s, he notes, it was IBM and the group called the BUNCH: Burroughs, UNIVAC, NCR, Control Data and Honeywell. He graduated in 1996 and interviewed in 1995. On-campus recruiting was active, and Microsoft was dominant. He decided, as a point of principle, that he would not work there.

followups.question: Why did you rule out Microsoft?
answer: Cantrill grew up in the personal-computer era of the 1980s. DOS had no memory protection, so a misbehaving application could reboot the machine and an unsaved English paper was gone. At university, which he entered in 1992, he learned that the microprocessor offered memory protection that DOS did not use. He says Windows did not use it either, though he adds that Windows is complicated.

Then he met Unix on a workstation. At 18 he had a shell, an FTP session, a compile and a game download all running at once in separate windows. He found that mind-bending. Looking back, he says Microsoft was not really an operating system company. In his view its core strength was compilers. He says the Mac of that period was cleaner but also lacked memory protection, which he found unconscionable.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

followups.question: What was the abuse, in short?
answer: Cantrill describes a pattern. Microsoft would announce that a promising company's application would become a feature of the operating system, and then the feature would not appear. He calls this vaporware and says Microsoft perfected it. He says Word was weak at first, improved over time, and displaced WordPerfect partly because Microsoft bundled it with the operating system.

He stresses that the anti-competitive behaviour was not only his opinion. He describes it as a judicial finding of fact. He adds that the company changed after the late-1990s antitrust case and as Gates reached middle age. He still would not have worked there.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: Your goodbye post said you did not particularly want to work for Sun. What changed your mind?
answer: Cantrill says the people he met in other Sun groups were fine but not energizing. He was used to being the youngest person in a group, but he wanted colleagues who shared his passion. Meeting Kevin Clark and Jeff Bonwick was, in his words, a bolt of lightning. Both were energized and saw the same potential for operating systems to be innovative. Both wanted to rip out broken code and replace it with beautiful code.
He remembers coming back from that trip certain that he would take an offer from Sun.
blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: What was the career ladder at Sun like?
answer: Cantrill describes the ladder as member of technical staff, staff engineer, senior staff engineer and distinguished engineer. He thinks Sun may have originated these titles, though Xerox PARC is another possibility. He is not sure.

He tells a story about business cards. Early on he did not know his rank and assumed that an engineer on staff was a staff engineer. Colleagues soon told him that would be like claiming tenure. He was an MTS3. Most college hires started at MTS2, but he says he was an unusual hire. He had done kernel development at a company in Canada for two summers. After school in the Northeast and work in Canada, he wanted to come out to Silicon Valley.
blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: What stands out in your growth from MTS3 to distinguished engineer?
answer: Cantrill says he never focused on grade, rank or promotion. He would rather be underpromoted than overpromoted, and he did not want to do work performatively. He did what he judged most important: solving customers' problems and making the operating system what he believed it could be. Sun, he says, was accommodating of headstrong engineers. In 1996 he thought Sun was the only company still invested in its own operating system, and work on the Solaris kernel was energizing. Promotions simply happened along the way.

He also reports a plain finding about formal reviews: they never made him perform better. In his view a review measures performance, while it should be about feedback that helps everyone be the best they can. He found the annual cadence broken. His reviews looked like his own self-review with grammatical errors added. The highlights of his career were never promotions. They were a significant body of work, a hard bug, or working with someone on something they thought impossible.

He describes Sun's rating tiers as superlative, excellent and good, with a rough split he recalls as about 70, 20 and 10 percent. A superlative rating forced a promotion, and Sun did not want promotions faster than every 18 months. So managers gave apologetic reviews that rated clearly better work as merely excellent. Cantrill says he did not care. He was promoted to staff engineer, by his estimate around 2001, just as the dot-com crash hit. The company bonus, which depended on company performance, was zero from then on.

Cantrill calls the process for becoming a distinguished engineer regrettable and stupid, though he is not describing his own promotion. He says there were two routes. One was a vote by existing distinguished engineers, which he calls a political process and a country club, and a bad place for democracy. The other was an acqui-hire in which the acquired company's CTO arrived with the title. He says people could tell the homegrown ones from the acqui-hired ones.

His own case, as he understands it second-hand, was presented by Sun's CTO, Greg Papadopoulos, who had chartered the Fishworks group that built a storage product. Papadopoulos reportedly said he expected no one to vote against it, and the vote was unanimous. Cantrill says he is grateful and did not want to deal with the politics. He sees ranks as corrosive, and Oxide has none.
blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: If an ambitious new graduate wants to become a distinguished engineer, should they focus on the work or ask their manager what the next level needs?
answer: Cantrill would steer them to a third path. He would ask why they want the title, since reaching it does not give meaning, and he calls it a recipe for a midlife crisis. He would try to find what drives meaning for that person and what fuels them. His aim is to stop them depending on external validation. He would introduce them to miserable distinguished engineers, and to miserable wealthy people, to show that the title or the money cannot be the answer. In his view, once the person finds the real driver, the work and the promotions follow.

followups.question: What if the mentee says they want financial independence?
answer: Cantrill first asks what that means in such a well-paid field. He points out that anyone in San Francisco can buy an excellent six-dollar coffee. If it means never needing to work for money again, he asks, what then? If the meaningful thing does not pay, he says to balance it with a career. He thinks it is a mistake to plan to reach independence first and pursue meaning afterwards.

He draws on the dot-com boom and bust. Most people around him made money on paper and lost it. He argues the bust helped, because people who had come for the money left and the rest had to remember why they came. He knew people who made fortunes in the boom, were not much interested in tech, and struggled in the next decade, wondering what to do. One bought several houses and found them a pain. He says too many people work in the industry only to leave it. His advice is to go and do the thing you would do after leaving. His example was quitting a job at Meta to become a podcaster, and the host answers that they did just that.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

followups.question: Does that match the posts from people who say they reached financial independence and do not know what to do now?
answer: Cantrill says the same problem appears in engineering even when the goal has meaning. He calls it postpartum engineering. When a team is focused on shipping something, shipping becomes the lens for everything. He feared this after Oxide shipped its first rack, when people who had pulled hard for a long time might ask what comes next. He adds that some people respond to the emptiness by chasing even more money. He names Larry Ellison as an example of a result people should not aspire to.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

followups.question: What about someone who is genuinely happy doing nothing?
answer: Cantrill jokes that anyone with a billion dollars would simply do that every day. He then tells a story about one of the earliest Yahoo employees he knew. This person was hired as a web surfer to help curate Yahoo's directory of links, in the era before search engines. The person received an equity grant on joining, never got another, and made a fortune. Cantrill says the person was never promoted, complained that the job was awful, and by the end owned only one topic, snowboarding in Northern California. He concludes that whatever this person found meaningful, it was not the work.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: Sun's ratings had no bad tier. Why not, and what do you think of stack ranking?
answer: Cantrill says Sun did not use performance improvement plans or the rank-and-yank approach Intel was known for, which is stack ranking. He calls stack ranking organizational cancer, especially when a bottom percentage is terminated. In his view it rewards managers for keeping dead weight on their teams, so that someone always ranks last.

He says this happened at Sun anyway. Someone once took him aside and said that a weak colleague was in his interest, because that person always received a good rating, which left room for others to receive excellent or superlative ones. Cantrill calls this a set of perverse incentives. His main objection is that stack ranking teaches people their teammates are adversaries. He believes teams do extraordinary things, that everyone should want to serve the team, and that stack ranking works against that.

followups.question: Sun's stock fell 98 percent. Was there no push for mass layoffs?
answer: Cantrill says the stock traded below the company's cash at one point. Sun resisted layoffs for a while, and Scott McNealy famously did not want to lay people off. Cantrill calls that a mistake and says McNealy waited too long. Once layoffs began, Cantrill recalls counting about 35 rounds over roughly eight years. Some were small, some large.

Employees could pull the staff directory programmatically from the internal organization tool. They ran a daily script they called the obits, which showed who had left. Some days it showed 1,500 or 3,000 people.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

followups.question: Was the company aware that you had that data?
answer: Cantrill says Sun's strength and weakness was that no one was truly in charge, so it would not have surprised him if people knew. He thinks Sun was a transparent company and that using the organization tool broke no policy. It was a way of knowing what was happening.

He adds that the whole industry was in the same position. He dates the dot-com collapse to the end of 2000, says September 11 made it worse, and says tech was basically dead for about five years. He places the founding of Y Combinator around 2006 and suggests it reflected a capital deficit, though he defers to Paul Graham on that. He calls the period bleak.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: Why was the Oracle acquisition of Sun so controversial?
answer: Cantrill says it was dramatic. He points to an SEC filing showing IBM and HP each trying to buy Sun and sabotage the other, partly to punish a competitor. Oracle then swept in. He does not see the acquisition itself as the controversial part. He sees Oracle as the issue. He says Oracle has little depth and compares it to an octopus that is good at feeding itself.

By contrast, he says Sun tried to do right by its customers and to solve hard technical problems with commercial relevance. It gave engineers great freedom and rewarded technical boldness. NFS, SPARC, Java, Solaris and the technologies he worked on all came from that passion and independence.

Cantrill says Sun often failed at business execution, so he hoped Oracle would bring that skill. He concluded he had overestimated Oracle. In his view Oracle focuses on its own profitability. It aims to gain something like a natural monopoly over its customers, suffocate competition and then raise the rent. He did not want to work for a company like that.

followups.question: In your 2011 talk you got through a slide without crying and said Oracle screws customers and lies. What is the lying?
answer: Cantrill says Oracle has made many promises to customers that it does not keep and has not earned their trust. He says that if you ask customers whether they trust Oracle, the answer is no. He adds that the slide he nearly cried over was about Sun, not Oracle. It carried Scott McNealy's epitaph for Sun: “Kicked butt, had fun, didn't cheat, loved our customers, changed computing forever.” That still chokes him up because he says it was true. Oxide adopted it as its own mission.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: Were top engineers confiding in one another that they had to leave Sun?
answer: Cantrill says it was less like confiding and more like running from a burning building. Before the deal closed, some employees were not going to become Oracle employees and would be laid off with rich severance. He describes a line of people wanting to be on the list. He says he was not one of them. He says some people still resent colleagues who left that way. He was at the Fishworks group in San Francisco and was somewhat optimistic that the best of both companies could be combined. He quit after about 45 days because he could not work there in good conscience.

followups.question: What did you see that made you leave so quickly?
answer: Cantrill says it was clear this was a very different company. After he decided to leave, he says, Oracle gave him several more reasons. The one he stresses is customer trust. Sun, for all its faults, had its customers' trust. They rooted for Sun to prevail because Sun was straight with them even when that did not serve its own interest. He says Oracle does not have that trust.

He realized he could not work for a company with such profound distrust. It eroded his sense of meaning. He felt ashamed to work at Oracle. At Sun he had sometimes felt embarrassed, but never ashamed.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

followups.question: How do you get yourself laid off?
answer: Cantrill says there is no web form. You tell your manager to put you on the list, or you whisper around to learn what is going on. He says it was not about underperformance. It was about saying that Oracle had no interest in your work. Then, he jokes, if Oracle shows interest in what you do, you are upset.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: You said Bezos is the apex predator of capitalism. What makes you say that?
answer: Cantrill, whose company Joyent competed with AWS, says Amazon at its height was relentless in execution. He says it hit the mother lode, and not only by luck. It allowed S3 to be developed, built EC2, and realized it was onto cloud computing before anyone else. He calls the re:Invent conferences from about 2010 to 2015 relentless. Each one brought price cuts and many new services, which customers loved.

He adds that Amazon did not break out AWS revenue and declined to discuss it with analysts. Cantrill says this helped spread the idea that cloud was a terrible business, so people stayed out. Joyent ran a public cloud and knew the margins were great. He says Amazon is no longer what it was in those years. He is not sure when the last re:Invent price cut was, but it has been a while.

followups.question: Why keep pressing instead of milking the market?
answer: Cantrill says Bezos is not merely a predator but an apex predator, and that is what made him so good. He pressed his advantage so no one could compete and no one wanted to enter the business. In Cantrill's view he did it the right way, by giving a great product at a reasonable price. Cantrill calls that a win-win and says it was essential for cloud-born companies in that era. He says it was very hard to compete with Amazon. Joyent had to find lanes where it could, and he calls the experience brutal given Amazon's extraordinary execution.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: What is the difference between VP of engineering and CTO?
answer: Cantrill gave a talk at Joyent on this contrast, but he is not sure how much he buys the difference now. In both roles you are an engineering leader. He says a CTO is more outward-looking, spending a lot of time on the road with customers, and jokes that the title could stand for chief travel officer. A VP of engineering tends to focus more on the mechanics of an engineering organization.

He joined Joyent as VP of engineering because the company already had a CTO, and he says he did not particularly care about titles, as at Sun. When the founding CTO left, he did care that the company not hire externally for the role. He later became CTO.

followups.question: Why not hire externally?
answer: Cantrill says an outside CTO was not what the company needed at that point. The company had removed its CEO and needed a terrific CEO, which he says it later got.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: What is the story behind starting your own company?
answer: Cantrill knew he wanted to start a company with Steve, who had come up on the sales and go-to-market side. Cantrill had not spoken to Steve before joining Joyent, and found him amazing once they worked together. They both felt they would do whatever came next together. Their long walks in San Francisco produced, in Cantrill's words, one bad idea after another. They then tried to find ideas investors would fund, which were not ideas from their hearts. He recommends that others not do this, though he says it is understandable.

The turning point came when Cantrill went to look up a prominent venture capitalist's email address. He had known this person since early in the person's career and had lunch with him periodically. The last email, about 18 months earlier, had said he would fund anything Cantrill put in front of him. Cantrill told Steve to go big and do what was in their hearts: build the computer they wanted, a rack-scale machine. Cantrill says this was in their marrow, after 14 years at Sun for him, a decade at Dell for Steve, and a decade together at Joyent. They envisioned rack-scale design, their own boards and switch, and all the software. A catalyst was seeing Facebook's Tioga Pass at the Open Compute summit, which he likens to discovering Unix after living with DOS. He says the idea was contrarian, and contrarian ideas appeal to venture investors.

After talking to many investors, he went back to that same one. About 45 seconds into the pitch the investor said that if this was a computer company, he wanted nothing to do with it. Cantrill pointed to the old email, and the investor replied that it did not sound like him. Cantrill says he expected the refusal. In his view, an investor who has had big zeros in a similar area is no longer blind to the odds, and this one had two big zeros, one resembling Oxide. When the investor asked how he could help, Cantrill had a concrete request: an introduction to the founders of that failed company. He advises always having an answer to that question.

The founder explained what went wrong. Cantrill says the company built something smaller than a rack, which he compares to very early Nitro. It found one customer, a huge bank, that wanted it only for around six Active Directory servers. The company raised money and hired a large sales team, and the market was too small for the team. It was acquired, but Cantrill says the founder was left bitter and felt the investors had put in too much capital at the wrong time. That founder called Oxide a “suicide mission.” Cantrill says he wrote the phrase in a notebook and underlined it.
blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: When I think of rack-scale compute these days I think of racks of GPUs. Are you building that?
answer: Cantrill says Oxide set out in 2019, when GPGPUs existed but were not the focus. The focus was general-purpose compute, storage and networking. He says people kept asking about accelerators. Oxide wants to build systems from first principles, with transparency at the hardware and software interface, and to write the lowest layer of software. Cantrill calls the product hardware and software co-design. He says that does not work with Nvidia, a proprietary company that executes well and wants to own the whole stack.

As he sees it, there were two doors, compete with Nvidia or partner with it, and he wanted neither. He adds that competing is becoming more plausible. So Oxide focused on general-purpose CPUs. He finds it surprising that the GPU field is crowded and gory, while on the CPU side HP, Dell and similar vendors keep selling the same thing, leaving Oxide alone with a hardware and software product. Customers who own many GPUs also own many CPUs, he says, because AI and high-performance workloads attach a lot of general-purpose compute to the special-purpose compute. He thinks Oxide will build an accelerator at some point. He says he has been calling it 18 months away for a while, and that it is not in the foreseeable future.
blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: In 1996, as a new graduate, you replied to a long technical post by David S. Miller with a personal jibe. What was the context, and what do you think now?
answer: Cantrill puts it firmly in the regret column. He says he has few regrets in his career. He was about 22 and had no idea the post would last 30 years. He explains that the jibe referred to an obscure Saturday Night Live sketch in which William Shatner, at a Star Trek convention, tells fans to get a life. He says that does not make it better, and he is not defending it. It was a mistake.

Miller had plenty to say in reply. Cantrill says he wrote a longer post taking Miller's points apart one by one. He has never met or talked to Miller, whom he calls a very talented person. He recalls reading in a book about Linux that Miller said a Sun engineer had put him back in his place. If that is Miller's account, Cantrill says it is generous to him. He hopes both of them regret it a little, as young and excitable people. He calls it a life lesson.
blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: In 2022 you tweeted that failure at a startup is almost always bad leadership, not the team. Does that apply to Sun, which ultimately failed?
answer: Cantrill does not remember writing the tweet, though he likes it and cannot recall what he was responding to. On Sun, he rejects the premise. Sun was founded in 1983 and was acquired around 2008 to 2009, by his dating. It was a public company in the Fortune 200. Many children went to college because their parents worked there. He says it did not succeed to the scope of its own ambition, but he regards Sun as a success, not a failure.

followups.question: Could different leadership have changed how Sun ended?
answer: Cantrill thinks so. He lists several reasons Sun did not survive as an independent company. It had become strung out on the high margins of the dot-com boom and never fully got off them. It embraced x86 too late. The company became fractured, and the layoffs did not help. He thought Fishworks could have been an exemplar of the products an independent Sun might develop, but that would have required leadership strongly interested in that change, and Sun did not have it.

In hindsight, he says, it was probably time for a change. He compares it to a forest fire in a healthy forest, which is part of the life cycle and allows rebirth. He concludes that Sun had succeeded, had run its course, and had its time.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: In 2022 you also wrote that Musk had no idea what he was doing at Twitter. Do you still agree?
answer: Cantrill says yes, and says he feels dirty being specific about it. He sees rampant bad behaviour on the platform. He credits Community Notes and describes nearly everything else as a tire fire.

followups.question: What is the number one problem?
answer: Cantrill says it is the reason Oxide does not engage on Twitter. He says he cannot have an Oxide post sitting next to some of the posts he has seen, which include extreme racism, antisemitism and anti-Islam hatred. He rejects the free-speech defence. He says the content is so deeply offensive that he does not want anyone looking at it and then at his company's content.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: You have lived through several booms and busts. What advice do you have for people in today's market?
answer: Cantrill says booms and busts are endemic to the industry. His grandfather was a petroleum engineer, so he grew up hearing about plants and pipelines built and then shut down as oil prices moved. When he moved out here he thought software was immune. He says it is not. He sees the swings as partly endearing, because the industry gets ahead of itself both in optimism and in pessimism.

His advice is to be careful about listening to others and to be your own judge. In 1996 people told him operating systems were done, and he is glad he did not listen. People said you could not start a computer company in 2019, and he is glad Oxide ignored them. He says the same applies to software-as-a-service today. There is truth in the claim that LLM-assisted coding will squeeze such companies, but if your heart is in it, treat both the pessimism and the optimism with a grain of salt. Do not choose a field because it is hot. He finds the current LLMs amazing, but says the reason to go in should be intrinsic. He closes by borrowing Steve Jobs's line about putting a dent in the universe.
blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: Almost everything in your career seems driven by fulfillment. Is there a time you would call the happiest?
answer: Cantrill says Oxide asks people when they have been happiest and why, for exactly this reason. For him it is not an era but moments, though he says he is pretty happy now. He recalls that a friend told him, during his walks with Steve, that he needed to answer why he wanted to start a company. It was not for financial return, which he says is not good life advice.

The answer was that his happiest moments came from working on a team where each person privately thought the task was too hard, and then everyone worked together, complimented one another and pulled it off. He had that feeling with the tracing work, at Fishworks, and a couple of times at Joyent, including the LX and Triton projects. Part of what drew him to Oxide's larger problem was the chance to attract such a team.

He says the organizational model for Oxide is a heist movie, with a safe cracker, a getaway driver and a demolitions expert, each skill arriving at the right moment. He and Steve share this team orientation, which he credits for how much Oxide has done with a small team.
blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: Looking back on your whole career, is there a top regret?
answer: Cantrill says he made an extraordinarily bad hire at Joyent, one he calls perhaps the worst hire in human history. He says the person had presented under an assumed name and had a serious criminal history, though he says that was not what made the person a bad employee. It was a bad experience, and also eye-opening, because he realized everything he had been doing about hiring was wrong.

After the situation was resolved, Joyent stripped hiring to the studs and rethought it from first principles. The result was a writing-intensive process that gets at intrinsic motivation, and it became the hiring process at Oxide. He says the extraordinary Oxide team is absolutely related to it, and he built it because he made the worst hire of all time. He says he needed that hire.

followups.question: So you don't regret it?
answer: Cantrill says he does not regret it. He would not go back and remove it, because he thinks Oxide does not exist otherwise. He would have kept hiring naively, without rigor, and not selecting for values. He says he views many failures this way, as important and hard to remove. If he had a time machine, he says, he might remove the Usenet post, which he thinks would have no long-lasting consequences, but little else.
followups.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill

blocks.question: If you could go back to the start of your career, what advice would you give yourself?
answer: Cantrill's answer is essentially not to mess anything up. He says he has been very lucky, in the right place at the right time many times, and that he trusted his gut when that was controversial. He would be scared to give his younger self advice, since he might tamper with a lucky career in which he worked with extraordinary colleagues. He says those colleagues have been essential to everything he has done.
He admits he made mistakes. He says the mistakes became load-bearing and important, and he would not want to remove them.
blocks.speaker: Bryan Cantrill
